claims.text: TLS runs on top of a transport that already delivers bytes reliably and in order, so it starts only after the TCP connection is open; on a first connection neither side sends application data before its own Finished message, so the browser asks for the page only after step 4.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 1 — TLS assumes a reliable, in-order byte stream from the layer beneath; section 2, the handshake precedes application data

claims.text: TLS authenticates the server to the client and encrypts what the two sides send after the handshake so only the two ends can read it; both sides' key material crosses the network readable, yet seeing both is not enough to build the keys.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 s1 — authentication; confidentiality: data after establishment only visible to the endpoints; s2 Figure 1 — key_share in ClientHello/ServerHello, before protection

claims.text: A certificate lists the names the server stands for, carries a public key made as a pair with the private key kept by the server, and states two dates between which it may be used.
claims.source_hint: RFC 5280 section 4.1 — subjectPublicKeyInfo, validity (notBefore/notAfter); section 4.2.1.6 subjectAltName

claims.text: A browser, as normally set up, passes the signer check only when the certificate's chain of signatures leads back to an authority already on the list its operating system or browser carries; a signature that does not lead back to that list does not pass that check.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 sections 4.3.3-4.3.4 — trust anchors and chain of trust; RFC 5280 section 6.1 — path validation starts from a trust anchor

claims.text: An `https` address means HTTP carried over a TLS connection, and its default port is 443 when the address does not name another one.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 section 4.2.2 — https URI scheme; TCP port 443 is the default when the port is not given

claims.text: The padlock names the browser's report that its checks on this connection passed; it is a statement about the connection only and does not judge who is behind the name or what the site does.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 sections 4.3.3 and 4.3.4 — what a client verifies before treating a connection as secured; no browser is pinned in versions.yaml

claims.text: The client names the site it wants in its first handshake message, because one machine on one port can hold certificates for several names and the server must be told which to send.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 4.2 and RFC 6066 section 3 — server_name is sent in ClientHello so a server hosting several names can pick a certificate

claims.text: In the usual setup, which the lab uses (it does nothing to hide the name), the name in that first message travels before encryption is in place, so anything on the path can read it.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 sections 1.2 and 4.1.2 — ClientHello precedes any protection; RFC 6066 section 11.1 — server_name is not protected

claims.text: Besides the server's signature over the exchange, a client checks three things it reads off the certificate: that it lists the name asked for, that the authority's signature leads to a trust anchor it holds, and that now is inside its two dates. A failure stops the page or asks the user to confirm.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 section 4.3.4 — obtain confirmation from the user or terminate the connection; RFC 5280 section 6.1 for the rest of path validation

claims.text: The certificate is public, sent to anyone who connects; each side contributes key material for the keys; the server signs the whole exchange with its private key, never sent, which the client checks with the certificate's public key, so a copied certificate cannot finish.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 s2 Figure 1 — key_share from both sides; CertificateVerify, signature over the entire handshake; RFC 9110 s4.3.3 — authority rests on using the private key (was claim 10)

claims.text: At the step drawn as 4, the client sends a value computed over the whole handshake it saw, confirming both ends have the same view of the messages and the same key.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 4.4.4 Finished — a MAC over the entire handshake, providing key confirmation

claims.text: In TLS 1.3 everything the server sends after its key material, the certificate included, is encrypted; the destination address and port, and normally the name asked for, stay visible, so an observer can usually list the sites opened but not the pages read.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 1.2 — all handshake messages after the ServerHello are encrypted; section 4.2 server_name in ClientHello

claims.text: In the lab, HTTPS is the `donhang.local:8443` block at the end of the `Caddyfile`; its `tls internal` line makes Caddy create an authority of its own and sign a certificate for that name, which the transcript prints as `issuer=CN=Caddy Local Authority - ECC Intermediate`.
claims.source_hint: Caddy docs, Caddyfile directive tls, `internal`; Caddyfile lines 93-99 and outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/inspect-cert.txt line 3 at stage-0

claims.text: Nothing in the lab puts Caddy's local authority on the reader's list: Caddy runs in a container of its own (service `web`) and tries to install its root only into that container's trust store, so the browser refuses the page while name and dates are valid.
claims.source_hint: Caddy docs automatic-https — root installed into the system's local trust store, may fail in containers; docker-compose.yml @stage-0, service `web`; no root install in repo

claims.text: The HTTPS block points `root` and `file_server` at `/srv/www`, the same folder the plain `:8080` site serves, so the same pages appear at both addresses (section 2); the fixed answers the `:8080` block adds, such as `/admin`, are not repeated there.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0: `root * /srv/www` at line 12 and line 97; docker-compose.yml mounts ./www at /srv/www

claims.text: A hosts-file line `127.0.0.1 donhang.local` points the name at the machine it is on. Caddy's container shares the lab box's addresses and ports, so on the lab box `127.0.0.1` port 8443 is Caddy listening, and the lab box's hosts file already has that line.
claims.source_hint: docker-compose.yml @stage-0: `lab` extra_hosts donhang.local:127.0.0.1, `web` network_mode service:lab; refs/docker-docs compose services.md; lesson foundation.l1.ip-and-ports

claims.text: `openssl s_client` opens a TLS connection and prints what came back, `openssl x509 -noout` prints only the fields named after it, and the `grep -E` stage keeps only the `Protocol` and `Cipher` lines.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/inspect-cert.txt (the three parts it prints) and scripts/network/inspect-cert.sh lines 7-19 at stage-0

claims.text: In the transcript the subject is empty and the name appears as `DNS:donhang.local` under `X509v3 Subject Alternative Name`, the field a client matches the name against; the dates print as `...` because the captured copy masks values that can change between runs; a live run prints them.
claims.source_hint: inspect-cert.txt lines 2, 4-5, 8-9; outputs/unstable.regex header (masked in every captured output only) and notBefore/notAfter lines; RFC 9110 s4.3.4 (DNS-ID)

claims.text: The two ends agree during the handshake on the version and on the other value the third part of the transcript prints, rather than either side assuming them; in the lab the version is `TLSv1.3`.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 4.1.3 — the server selects version and cipher suite from what the client offered; inspect-cert.txt lines 12-13

claims.text: The script prints the certificate of a site a browser refuses, because nothing in it stops on a signer it does not accept; the lab box's own list does not carry Caddy's authority either.
claims.source_hint: scripts/network/inspect-cert.sh lines 3, 7-19 at stage-0 — no -verify_return_error or -CAfile; docker-compose.yml — caddy-data volume mounted into `web` only

claims.text: A refusing program ran the checks and knows which failed; TLS also defines separate error codes, sent to the other end, for an expired certificate and for an unaccepted signer.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 s4.3.4 — the user agent itself terminates the connection with a bad certificate error; RFC 8446 s6.2 — alerts certificate_expired and unknown_ca

claims.text: A passing check says the server holds the private key for the name asked for; none of the client's checks looks at who is behind the name or what the site does with what it receives.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 sections 4.3.3 and 4.3.4 — validation binds a key to an identifier; no clause concerns the operator's conduct

claims.text: A certificate stops being valid at its later date whether or not anything changed, so when nobody is responsible for replacing it in time, the failure is a date that was always coming, not bad luck.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 6.2 — certificate_expired; RFC 5280 section 4.1.2.5 — validity notBefore/notAfter

claims.text: When a certificate check fails, the browser does not show the page: it either stops the connection or asks the user to confirm before going on.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 section 4.3.4 — obtain confirmation before proceeding or terminate the connection; warning wording is in no pinned source

claims.text: An authority whose certificates browsers accept is expected to sign a certificate for a name only after checking that whoever asks controls that name, which is what ties the name to the public key in the certificate.
claims.source_hint: Caddy docs automatic-https, ACME challenges — a publicly-trusted cert requires validation by the authority; it checks the name's DNS or a resource served there before issuing

beyond_scope: Names the `subjectAltName` field and says the name check reads it rather than the subject, because the captured output prints an empty `subject=`.
The captured output prints a cipher suite name; the prose does not explain it ("one more line a later lesson explains"), so depth_notes hold.
Says the captured dates print as `...` because the printed copy masks values that can change between runs, while a live run prints real dates.

Says an authority on the list is expected to sign for a name only after checking that the asker controls it (claim 26), because without it the signer check does not explain why a listed signature ties name to key.
Names 443 as the default https port, because the lab uses 8443 and the reader would otherwise take 8443 as the normal one.
